newsitem.title: UK: Police attacked afer finding N.Ireland bomb.
newsitem.headline: Police attacked afer finding N.Ireland bomb.

text.p: Catholics youths threw petrol bombs and stones early on Monday at police searching a housing estate where the ingredients for a huge home-made bomb, a favoured weapon of IRA guerrillas, were found on Sunday.
"It was just one step away from being fully functional," said a police spokesman in Londonderry, where the explosives were found. "It was meant to be planted and it was meant to cause death."

The explosives, which needed only a detonator to be primed for use, were discovered 48 hours before Northern Ireland peace talks resume in Belfast still awaiting word whether the IRA will call the truce necessary to admit its Sinn Fein political wing.
Around 300 lbs (140 kg) of the substance was found on Sunday in three plastic bins in a coal shed at the back of a house in a staunch Irish nationalist estate of the province's second city.
Another two bags of explosives were found as police evacuated 50 houses and searched the area into the night.
Mitchell Mclaughlin, the Sinn Fein chairman, said the Londonderry bomb would be followed by others unless Britain eased its conditions for the party's entry to the talks.
"Unless we bring about a resolution to the conflict, it will happen again," he told BBC radio.

He said Britain had to convince Sinn Fein the peace talks would not be bogged down by demands that the Irish Republican Army surrender the weapons it has used in a 28-year war against British rule of the province.
Sinn Fein also wanted reassurance that the talks would be credible and not be open-ended. "We want to see all of this resolved," McLaughlin said.
The laborious negotiations between pro-British Unionists and pro-Irish nationalists resume on Tuesday to clear the way for discussion of substantive issues in September.

Britain last month reopened contact with Sinn Fein which it broke off after the IRA ended a truce in February 1996. But the talks were broken off again after the IRA murdered two policeman in a daylight shooting in Lurgan.
A British government source confirmed a report in the Irish Times that written exchanges between the two sides were continuing. Further details were not available.
Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary, Mo Mowlam, said at the weekend that Sinn Fein could join the negotiations six weeks after an IRA ceasefire if it was deemed credible.
The London government has accepted proposals that guerrillas disarm while the talks progress, rather than to gain entry to the negotiations, its former position.

Ian Paisley, leader of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party was critical: "If the IRA declare another bogus ceasefire it can get to the talks immediately without handing in a gun or a murder weapon or repudiating violence."
Protestant Unionists loyal to British rule dismissed hopes of a new IRA truce as "wishful thinking".

"The reality is that Sinn Fein/IRA are committed to violence in order to achieve objectives that no democrat can support," said David Trimble, the head of Northern Ireland's biggest pro-British group, the Ulster Unionist party.
Hopes of progress had risen after the Orange Order scrapped four parades over the weekend that had been routed through Catholic areas and were likely to spark rioting.
The marches reached a climax on Saturday, the most cherished date in the Orange Order calendar which marks a 1690 victory by King William of Orange over Catholic King James the second.
The parades, which are marked by a public holiday, passed off relatively peacefully, police said.
But security forces came under attack in Belfast overnight when they tried to end clashes between pro-British Loyalists and Catholics who attacked each other for the second night.
